what_i_got_wrong:
⛔ THE FILING'S PLACEMENT ADVICE WAS HALF WRONG AND I SHIPPED THE WRONG HALF FIRST — caught by running it, not by reading it. AUT-PD-143 said place the pass LAST; I reasoned it should run mid-pipeline so each penalty would be charged by its owning pass, and the dry run showed RT-PARTNER-STRAT rows entering at 195.86. Diagnosed rather than guessed: mid-pipeline the floor is a PRE-penalty value, so it read 195.0 for a sibling (AUT-049) the ledger shows at 105.0 — a `_score_basis` citing a number that appears nowhere in the file, and five sandbox process defects entering ABOVE the live research the pass exists to surface. Caught by re-fetching before committing rather than after: origin/main had moved 73ba69ef6 → 19be84298 and one of those commits, AUT-PD-050, had diagnosed the SAME defect concurrently and landed its ordering and crash halves. ⭐ The duplication was real and only partly avoidable — AUT-PD-050's row was `in_progress` under SEAT-s6-1f1a2449 when this cycle chose its item, so the collision was visible in the ledger and I did not look at what the in-progress rows were about before taking a queued row in the same family. The overlapping half was DROPPED rather than re-filed, and only the genuinely new half (what RT-AUTONOMY is in systems/graph) went in, as AUT-PD-147.
⛔ AND THE TRUNK MOVED A SECOND TIME, 8 MORE COMMITS, WHILE THE FINAL GATE RAN. A concurrent session regenerated the same drifted view (197770ccc) — the SYMPTOM — without the pyyaml cause, making this cycle's regeneration redundant and its workflow fix the only part that stops the recurrence. Ids were counted explicitly after this rebase too, and BOTH ids allocated at the first rebase (AUT-PD-147, AUT-PD-148) had been taken in the interval; they are re-filed as AUT-PD-152 and AUT-PD-153 with `_renamed_from` recorded. The explicit count caught a collision at BOTH rebases, which is the whole of AUT-PD-144's argument.
⛔⛔ AND THE WORST ERROR OF THE CYCLE WAS MINE AND NEARLY SILENT: THE LANDING SCRIPT DROPPED A LEDGER ROW AND EVERY DOWNSTREAM CHECK STILL PASSED. Re-applying this cycle's edits keyed on ID. The ids were renumbered THREE times as concurrent sessions took them, so on the last rebase the script found AUT-PD-154 present and filed by this cycle, called it 'already applied', and moved on — but what sat at that id was this cycle's OTHER row from an earlier numbering. Result: the publish-regen row duplicated under two ids and the RT-AUTONOMY judgement row DROPPED, with NO duplicate id for the id-check to catch and nothing else looking. Caught only by reading the two rows' text and noticing they were identical. ⭐ FIXED BY KEYING ON IDENTITY, NOT ID: each row carries a `_cycle_row_key`, the re-apply matches on that, refuses when a key's id has moved under it, refuses when an id is taken by another filer, and asserts key-uniqueness beside the duplicate-id assert. ⚠ THE GENERAL LESSON IS THE ONE THIS REPOSITORY KEEPS RE-LEARNING: an id is not an identity when ids get reallocated, and a check that can only see duplicates cannot see a deletion.

⭐ THE BAR WAS NEVER BENT. CLAUDE.md §6's 'the run you report green must be the run that saw the tree you commit' does not bend, and the tempting shortcut — push after a mechanical rebase because the resolution 'looks safe' — is exactly AUT-PD-144's incident. The landing loop re-gates instead, every time.
⭐ WHAT ACTUALLY FIXED IT WAS SHRINKING THE DIFF, NOT LOOSENING THE GATE. `priority.py --write` re-sorts and re-scores the whole ledger, so this cycle's four SEMANTIC edits (close one row, annotate one, file two) were landing as a 1,207-line diff that conflicted with every concurrent write. Committing the semantic edits WITHOUT the regeneration takes it to 75 lines. The generated ordering is not lost: it is regenerated by the next cycle's step 3, which is what generates it anyway. ⚠ A generated file committed alongside a semantic edit makes every concurrent session a conflict; that is the general lesson and it is filed.
